newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Asia stocks weaker, yen hits Tokyo, Seoul.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Asia stocks weaker, yen hits Tokyo, Seoul.

text.p: Most Asian stock markets shrugged off Wall Street's latest record close and turned lower on Wednesday, as a rising yen hurt markets in Japan and South Korea.
News of a more than 90 percent rise in Japan's politically sensitive current account surplus was as analysts expected and sent barely a ripple through financial markets.

But U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers warned Japan to avoid running up external surpluses, prompting the U.S. dollar to fall sharply to its lowest level since November 20, 1996. The greenback touched 110.97 yen before recovering to around 111.45 yen. It had closed at 112.17/20 yen in New York on Tuesday.
"Investors are keeping a low profile...and on top of that, the yen/dollar rate moved to a level which could not be ignored and selling emerged," a trader at a foreign brokerage said.
Japan's key 225-share Nikkei index was off 242.62 points, or 1.18 percent, at 20,289.93 in afternoon trading.
The yen's rise also hurt South Korean stocks, leaving the composite index down 4.04 points, at 765.79.
On Tuesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average zoomed past the 7,500 level for the first time to end up 60.77 points at 7539.27 -- the third straight record finish for blue chip stocks.
Analysts said the gains were made in a market awash in cash, much of it coming from international investors fleeing the uncertainties of the European Monetary Union (EMU).

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index bucked the Asian trend, rising 105.76 points, or 0.73 percent, at 14,5545.47 around midday. The market did an about-face after initially dropping 1.06 percent in early trading as property stocks, utilities and China-related shares fell victim to profit-taking.
"Rumours and bad news on properties, red chips and H-shares expedited the pace of the price fall," said Peter Lui, in institutional sales at NAVA SC Securities.

Philippine stocks tacked on modest gains, bolstered by the Dow's advance and the Supreme Court's decision to reject a petition to change the constitution to allow President Fidel Ramos to seek a second term.
There had been fears that a ruling in Ramos's favour would spark protests.
The main index ended 12.63 points, or 0.46 percent, higher at 2,787.74.
Thai stocks were hit following the central bank's latest moves to prevent foreigners from repatriating baht funds obtained through stock trading.
Bangkok's main index was off 4.98 points, or 0.94 percent, at 522.24.
Taiwan stocks fell sharply after opening mixed as profit-taking dragged down the electronics sector, considered a bellweather for the market.
The index closed down 125.98 points, or 1.5 percent, at 8,267.00.
Indonesian shares were off 2.33 points, or 0.34 percent at 687.439, while Malaysian shares shed 4.56 points, or 0.41 percent to stand at 1,105.80.
Singapore's Straits Times Index was off 16.47 points, or 0.82 percent, at 1,999.31 and Australia's All Ordinaries Index lost 15.2 points, or 0.58 percent, to 2,613.7.
In New Zealand, a sharp gain in shares of Telecom and a solid improvement in the forestry sector hoisted the New Zealand share market. It closed 17.42 points higher at 2,384.97.
